highest conversion with 8–28% Cu
props.statement: The highest conversion of CO2 to methanol was obtained with catalysts containing 8–28% Cu + 92–72% Al2O3, giving 94% at 410 atm and a catalyst temperature of 285°.

props.name: CO + H2 gives only 39–43% methanol with methane and dimethyl ether
props.statement: With carbon monoxide and hydrogen over copper-alumina catalysts (expts. 14–16), under conditions similar to those with CO2, methanol conversion was only 39–43%, while 10–15% and 32–41% of the CO charged gave methane and dimethyl ether.

props.name: adding CO2 almost eliminates ether and raises methanol
props.statement: Replacing only 25% of the carbon monoxide with carbon dioxide (expts. 17, 18) almost completely eliminated ether formation; at CO:CO2 = 3.1:1.0 methanol conversion rose to 64% and dimethyl ether fell to about 1%.

props.name: copper and alumina separately inactive; the mixture is necessary
props.statement: Copper and alumina, separately, did not catalyze methanol formation from carbon dioxide and hydrogen; the mixture of the two is necessary.

props.name: lower pressure reduces conversion; reaction stops at CO
props.statement: Lowering the pressure (expts. 10–12) from 409 to 117 atm reduced conversion from 94 to about 13%, the reaction at the lower pressures tending to stop with the reduction of the dioxide to the monoxide.

props.name: H2:CO2 ratio does not change the product type; methanol falls with less hydrogen
props.statement: Changing the hydrogen:carbon dioxide ratio (expts. 7–9) did not materially influence the type of products; the methanol yield fell off due to the decrease in the limiting reactant, hydrogen.

props.name: heat released in CO reduction causes methanol dehydration to ether
props.statement: In the CO experiments (expts. 14–16) the energy released caused catalyst temperatures about 30° above the furnace, and this energy caused dehydration of nascent methanol to dimethyl ether; no comparable release occurs with CO2 because the reduction of CO2 to CO is endothermic.

props.name: higher temperature lowers methanol conversion and raises methane and CO
props.statement: With the 62% Cu catalyst, increasing temperature (expts. 3–6) lowered the conversion to methanol from 85 to about 2% and increased conversion to methane and carbon monoxide from about 1% to 44 and 14%, respectively.

props.name: water experiments inconclusive
props.statement: Experiments with water (not tabulated) were inconclusive: ether formation was eliminated, but methanol conversion fell to about 4% and 62% of the CO charged reacted with water to form CO2.

props.name: CO2 → CO → formaldehyde → methanol via Cannizzaro on amphoteric alumina
props.statement: Methanol forms from carbon dioxide and hydrogen by initial reduction of CO2 to CO with formation of water, reaction of hydrogen with CO to formaldehyde, and conversion of formaldehyde, in the presence of amphoteric aluminum oxide, to methanol and formic acid by the Cannizzaro reaction (2HCHO + H2O → CH3OH + HCOOH); the formic acid decomposes to H2 + CO2 or H2O + CO.

props.name: two paths: direct hydrogenation of formaldehyde and the Cannizzaro reaction
props.statement: After reduction of carbon dioxide through carbon monoxide to the formaldehyde stage, part of the methanol is formed by direct hydrogenation of the formaldehyde and part by the Cannizzaro reaction.

props.name: water formed from CO2 reduction, or CO2 itself, hinders ether formation
props.statement: The presence of water formed on reduction of carbon dioxide, or the carbon dioxide itself, may hinder the formation of methyl ether, explaining why no dimethyl ether forms from CO2 and hydrogen.
